about: CHAIN saga_england_south_east: THE NINE SHIPS (Design/content/CHAINS.md; page Design/content/chains/saga_england_south_east.md; words Data/writing/chain_saga_england_south_east.json). The saga of the south-east in the years when the heathen men first stayed the winter on Thanet: Ealdorman Ealhhere of Kent, the ship fight at Sandwich (851) and the fight on the island (853) where he and Huda of Surrey died. Played at Sarre, Fordwic, Dofras, Lundenwic, Hamwic, Gipeswic and Dommoc, October 850 to 856. Fourteen cards. Step flags ch_saga_england_south_east_1 .. _10 (every later step asks only for _1 and its own window, so a missed step is never a dead end). Side flags: _watch (counted sails for the ealdorman), _asked, _creek (took the camp's order), _told, _nuns (carried the sisters), _warned_wic, _pilot, _supply, _led, _book, _gave_book, _sworn, _tide (set to 8: it is the 'by' of the chance in step 10), _lives, _fell, _carried, _shore, _camp. Endings: ch_saga_england_south_east_end_fallen (what happened), _end_lives (history changed: changed_thanet_853), _end_creek (the camp's man), _end_minster (the sisters' shipman). Every ending also sets ch_saga_england_south_east_done. Lasting costs: ch_saga_england_south_east_marked_by_fleet, ch_saga_england_south_east_kent_remembers. Every option's note names its outcome text. Written 6 Oct 2026; a draft for the user to overwrite.

cards.note: Step 1, the start (drawn at Sarre, Fordwic or Dofras from October 850 to May 851). The toll man asks whom you mean to sell to; the ealdorman stands behind him. Sources: 'The heathens now for the first time remained over winter in the Isle of Thanet' (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 851, tr. J. Ingram 1823; the winter is taken as 850 to 851 (?)); Ealhhere, ealdorman of Kent, named 839 to 853, given forty hides at Lenham by King Aethelwulf in 850 (Wikipedia 'Ealhhere', the charter not read (?)); the king's toll at Sarre and Fordwic (Sawyer 29, dossiers/sarre.md); the beat 'whom do you mean to sell to' is places/sarre.json, story sarre.nine_sails. People: sarre.ealhhere (historical; the role 'chief' as in places/sarre.json); the toll man is the port's. That an ealdorman asked a merchant to count sails is ours (?). Sets ch_saga_england_south_east_1; _watch or _asked.

cards.title: Whom do you mean to sell to
cards.intention: The toll man does not ask what you carry. He asks whom you mean to sell to. A big man in a red cloak stands behind him and listens to the answer.

options.label: Go up at first light and count sails for him
options.note: outcome: chain_saga_england_south_east.s01.out_down (costs a morning; 20 d and half toll for a month)

options.label: Say you sell on the strand, in daylight, where the toll man can see
options.note: outcome: chain_saga_england_south_east.s01.out_strand (costs nothing)

options.label: Ask what an army on an island pays for bread
options.note: outcome: chain_saga_england_south_east.s01.out_ask (costs pride and the ealdorman's ease; the price word is true: the island eats, and corn is dear on the strait)

memory.strand: said he sold only on the strand
memory.ask: asked what the camp paid for bread

cards.note: Step 2 (scheduled a day after step 1 at Sarre; also drawn there to June 851). A buyer from the camp wades out at dusk. Sources: the wintering on Thanet (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 851); an army that winters must be fed, and armies of these years bought as well as took (the peace-and-payment of 865 on Thanet, Chronicle 865; the market the Northmen held on the Seine island in 861, Annals of St Bertin (?)); cut silver by weight is the Danes' money (BRIEF.md rule 2). The beat is places/sarre.json, story sarre.nine_sails. Ketil is invented (a common Norse name). Sets ch_saga_england_south_east_2; _creek if the order is taken, _told and _watch if the creek is given away.

cards.title: The creek and the tide
cards.intention: At dusk a man wades out over the saltings to your boat, up to the thigh, holding a small folding balance above the water. He speaks like a Dane and names a creek and a tide.

options.label: Take his order: six sacks of wheat to the creek within the month
options.note: outcome: chain_saga_england_south_east.s02.out_sell (30 d of cut silver in earnest and an order at three times the strand's price; somebody may have seen the boat)

options.label: Hear him out, then give the ealdorman's man the creek and the tide
options.note: outcome: chain_saga_england_south_east.s02.out_tell (25 d from the reeve; the creek is watched and the buyer knows who talked)

options.label: Say your corn is spoken for, and wish him a dry walk home
options.note: outcome: chain_saga_england_south_east.s02.out_no (costs nothing; what he let fall about the camp is true and goes on the board)

memory.sell: took the camp's order for wheat
memory.tell: gave the creek away to the ealdorman
memory.no: said his corn was spoken for

cards.note: Step 3 (scheduled two days after step 1 at Sarre; also drawn there to June 851). A sister of the minster on the island asks for a passage for the books, the plate and the youngest. Sources: Minster-in-Thanet, St Mary's and the church of Peter and Paul with St Mildrith's body; its ships toll-free at Sarre and Fordwic, one 'lately built in the minster' (Sawyer 29, Sawyer 91; dossiers/sarre.md); the nuns of Lyminge were given a refuge inside Canterbury in 804 (Sawyer 160; chronicle_793.json), which is the precedent the sister names; Asser about 893 still knows a minster on Thanet, so the house was not destroyed in these years (dossiers/sarre.md section 8). The abbess of 850 is not known and is not named. Beornwynn is invented (Beorn- + -wynn). That anything was sent off the island in 850 is ours (?). Sets ch_saga_england_south_east_3; _nuns if they are carried. The Turn is paid here: the carriage money and a riddle.

cards.note: Step 4 (scheduled twenty days after step 1 at Lundenwic; drawn there from February to June 851). The open beach before the storm: the host of the Frisians' yard and the Mercian king's wic-reeve. Sources: 'great slaughter in London' (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 839 for 842, Ingram 1823); the 350 ships that stormed London in 851 and put King Beorhtwulf of the Mercians to flight (Chronicle 851); the ditches dug across the roads of the wic after 851 (places/lundenwic.json, era 842 to 870); Lundenwic is Mercian in these years (ports_793.json). People: lundenwic.ceolmund (invented in places/lundenwic.json from the plot name Ceolmundingchaga, Sawyer 208); the reeve is King Beorhtwulf's, invented and unnamed. That Kent sent its count of sails to London is from the tie in places/lundenwic.json and is ours (?). Sets ch_saga_england_south_east_4; _warned_wic if the yard is warned.

host.note: lundenwic.ceolmund, who keeps the Frisians' yard by the west road

cards.title: An open beach
cards.intention: The Strand is as open as it ever was: no bank, no ditch, booths down to the tide line. Your host wants to know what is on Thanet. The reeve wants to know why it should be his trouble.

options.label: Tell Ceolmund what a wintered fleet does in spring, and help him bury the yard's silver and weights
options.note: outcome: chain_saga_england_south_east.s04.out_warn (costs a day's selling; it is remembered in steps 5 and 9)

options.note: outcome: chain_saga_england_south_east.s04.out_trade (costs nothing; the price word is true: Kent's corn is not coming up the river this spring)

memory.count: brought the count of sails from Kent
memory.trade: sold his goods and said it was not his beach

cards.note: Step 5 (drawn at Hamwic or Dofras from July to October 851). After the storm: the king's men want ships in the water, and a shipwright from the Dour is buying tar and looking for a man who knows the south mouth of the Wantsum. Sources: 'The same year came three hundred and fifty ships into the mouth of the Thames; the crew of which went upon land, and stormed Canterbury and London; putting to flight Bertulf, king of the Mercians'; 'Ethelwulf and his son Ethelbald, at the head of the West-Saxon army, fought with them at Ockley, and made the greatest slaughter of the heathen army that we have ever heard reported to this present day' (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 851, tr. Ingram 1823; chronicle_793.json 851-thanet-canterbury-london); Hamtun is the king's vill (Sawyer 288, dossiers/hamwic.md) and a near-empty shore by 851 (places/hamwic.json); boats are built up the Dour at Dofras (places/dofras.json, dofras.sheds). King Aethelstan, under-king of Kent 839 to 851, is King Aethelwulf's son. Where the ships of the Sandwich fight were found or fitted is not recorded: Hamwic and the Dour are ours (?). Wihtgar is invented (Wiht- + -gar). Sets ch_saga_england_south_east_5; _pilot or _supply.

cards.note: Step 6 (drawn at Sarre or Fordwic from August to November 851). The ship fight at Sandwich. Sources: 'The same year King Athelstan and Alderman Elchere fought in their ships, and slew a large army at Sandwich in Kent, taking nine ships and dispersing the rest' (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 851, tr. Ingram 1823, read 6 Oct 2026 at avalon.law.yale.edu/medieval/ang09.asp): the first fight at sea in English record. Sandwich (Sondwic) is first named in this annal and lies at the south mouth of the Wantsum (dossiers/sarre.md). The season is not recorded: the chain puts it about Michaelmas, when a fleet goes home laden (?). Whether it came before or after the storming of Canterbury is not certain, the copies of the Chronicle order the year differently (?). King Aethelstan is not heard of after this year. People: King Aethelstan of Kent (historical), sarre.ealhhere (historical), Wihtgar (invented). Sets ch_saga_england_south_east_6; _led if the player steers. Schedules step 7.

options.note: outcome: chain_saga_england_south_east.s06.out_lie_up (costs nothing; the price word is true: Canterbury was stormed and has no corn)

cards.note: Step 7 (scheduled forty days after step 6 at Gipeswic; drawn at Gipeswic or Dommoc from October 851 to the end of 852). A psalter out of Canterbury, its boards stripped, for sale on the East Angles' shore. Sources: Canterbury stormed in 851 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 851); books carried off for their covers and bought back with gold (the Old English inscription in the Stockholm Codex Aureus, where Ealdorman Alfred and his wife Waerburh say they bought the book from the heathen army 'with pure gold' and gave it to Christ Church, mid ninth century; our words, not a quotation, from Wikipedia 'Stockholm Codex Aureus' through dossiers/fordwic.md); Bishop Aethelwald of Dommoc swore obedience to Archbishop Ceolnoth in writing (Haddan and Stubbs III, pp. 659-660; places/dommoc.json, dommoc.aethelwald); Frisians under Rorik at Dorestad from 850 deal with the fleets (chronicle_793.json 850-rorik-dorestad; cast.rorik). This psalter and its seller are ours (?). Folcbald is invented (Folc- + -bald). Sets ch_saga_england_south_east_7; _book if it is bought.

cards.note: Step 8 (drawn at Fordwic through 852). The year between: Canterbury mends its roofs, the archbishop's clerk takes back what comes back, and the ealdorman says where he is going next summer and tells merchants to keep off the strait that day (the warning before the danger of step 10). Sources: Ceolnoth, archbishop of Canterbury 833 to 870 (dossiers/fordwic.md); Canterbury stormed 851; the refuge of Lyminge's sisters inside the wall, 804 (Sawyer 160); the Codex Aureus ransom as in step 7; the writing room of Christ Church writes a worse hand each year (places/fordwic.json, era 826 to 850). The clerk Wigbeorht is invented (Wig- + -beorht). The reckoning over the creek is ours. Sets ch_saga_england_south_east_8; _gave_book; _sworn if the player owns to the creek and swears off the camp. The Turn is paid here for the book.

cards.note: Step 9 (drawn at Lundenwic from January to June 853). Huda, ealdorman of Surrey, is over the river at the wic buying for a march into Kent, and asks a man who knows the strait how wide the water is. Sources: 'Elchere with the men of Kent, and Huda with the men of Surrey, fought in the Isle of Thanet with the heathen army' (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 853, tr. Ingram 1823); the fleet of 851 'marched southward over the Thames into Surrey' (Chronicle 851), so Surrey had its own score; ditches two metres deep dug across the roads of the wic after 851 (places/lundenwic.json); the Wantsum 'fordable only in two places' (Bede I.25, tr. L. C. Jane 1903). Nothing is known of Huda but this annal: his words and his coming to Lundenwic are ours (?). People: Huda (historical); lundenwic.ceolmund. Sets ch_saga_england_south_east_9; _tide (to 8: it is the stat of the chance in step 10) if the player tells him how the water runs.

cards.note: Step 10, the turn of the whole chain (drawn at Sarre from June to September 853). The men of Kent and Surrey go over to the island at the ebb. Sources: 'Elchere with the men of Kent, and Huda with the men of Surrey, fought in the Isle of Thanet with the heathen army, and soon obtained the victory; but there were many men slain and drowned on either hand, and both the aldermen killed' (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 853, tr. Ingram 1823; the first half read 6 Oct 2026 at avalon.law.yale.edu, the second half as places/sarre.json has it); the oldest copy says they had the victory 'at first' (?). The season is not recorded: 'after the hay' is ours (?). 'Drowned' is read here as the tide coming back over the ford of the Wantsum, which is ours and likely (Bede I.25 for the two fords; dossiers/sarre.md for the strait). The warning was given in step 8 and is given again here by the ferryman. The chance of the option 'ford' is read by the flag ch_saga_england_south_east_tide (8 if the player told Huda how the water runs in step 9: sure; 0 if not: doubtful). People: sarre.ealhhere, Huda (historical); the ferryman is the port's. Sets ch_saga_england_south_east_10 and one of _lives, _fell (+ _carried), _shore, _camp; schedules the ending.

cards.note: Ending 1, WHAT HAPPENED (scheduled five days after step 10 at Sarre; drawn at Sarre or Fordwic to 856; it also comes to a player who was elsewhere on the day, from October 853). Both ealdormen are dead on the island and the heathen men are still there; in 855 they winter on Sheppey (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 853 and 854 for 855, Ingram 1823). Sources for the people: Ealhhere's sister Ealhburh and his brother Aethelmod, who is ealdorman of Kent after him, are known from Kentish charters of about 850 to 860 (from memory, not checked tonight (?)); the gilded cup is places/sarre.json (sarre.ealhhere 'looks', and the ending 'watchman' of story sarre.nine_sails, where a widow sends it: here it is the sister, since no wife is recorded). The steward Osferth is invented (Os- + -ferth). Rewards: unlock_heirloom_ealhheres_cup, unlock_charter_sarre, or both by the hard road (the player who carried the body over). Sources: the heathen men winter on Sheppey in 855 (Anglo-Saxon Chronicle 854 for 855); the Norse felag, a sworn partnership of purse and boat (CHAINS.md; the word is on later rune stones); cut silver by weight. cards.note: Ending 4, THE SISTERS' SHIPMAN (scheduled five days after step 10 at Sarre; drawn at Sarre or Fordwic to 856). The player lay under the minster's shore on the day of the fight and took off the sisters who had stayed and the hurt of both shires. History as it happened; the minster outlives these years (Asser, about 893, still knows it). Sources: the minster's ships free of toll at Sarre and Fordwic, and a worn-out ship replaced by another under the same freedom (Sawyer 29, dossiers/fordwic.md); the abbess's ship lent to a trusted master (places/sarre.json, ships: coaster_minster_ship); cloths laid on a saint's tomb and given as relics are the custom of the age (Gregory of Tours, Glory of the Martyrs 27, from memory (?)); St Mildrith's body stays at Minster until 1030. The abbess is not named: she is not known. Beornwynn is invented.
